post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: The EU's output of law is explained by informal incentives: Commission, rapporteurs, committees and rotating Council Presidencies are all rewarded for producing legislation, and closed-door trilogues 'manufacture' consensus in advance, so the system expands EU law despite its many formal veto points.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: Between 2019 and 2024 the EU passed about 13,000 acts (about seven per day), against roughly 3,500 pieces of legislation and 2,000 resolutions from the US Congress over the same period.
verified: original source checked (Draghi Part A, ch. on regulation: 'around 3,500 pieces of legislation ... around 2,000 resolutions ... around 13,000 acts', 2019-2024)

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: The European Parliament has 705 members drawn from roughly 200 national parties; the Council represents 27 governments; laws need a double qualified majority.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: The EU budget is around 1% of GDP, about one-third earmarked for agriculture and one-third for regional aid, so for the Commission 'policy equals legislation'.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: Trilogues (informal, not in the Treaties, formalised by a 2007 declaration) now decide law privately; the final AI Act trilogue lasted nearly 38 hours, which the author links to drafting errors.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: A slim committee majority can drive major policy: the ENVI committee approved the 100% CO2 cut for new cars by 2035 by just 6 votes, and plenary adopted it as its mandate less than four weeks later.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: Council Presidencies rotate every six months, with a 13-year wait before a state holds it again, which pushes Presidencies to close deals fast.

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: A BusinessEurope analysis of 13 EU laws found 169 cases where different laws regulate the same issue; in almost a third the requirements differed and in about one in ten they were contradictory.
original_source: BusinessEurope gap analysis, cited in Draghi report, Part A (2024), https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/97e481fd-2dc3-412d-be4c-f152a8232961_en
verified: original source checked (Draghi Part A: '13 pieces of EU law flagged duplication across 169 requirements, including differences (29%) and outright inconsistencies (11%)')

post_title: How Brussels writes so many laws
text: There is no aggregate check on burden: the Standard Cost Model is applied unevenly, Parliament and Council amendments get no cost-benefit analysis, and no single method assesses EU law once transposed nationally.

EU reporting and compliance rules (CSRD, deforestation, GDPR, AI Act) are building a self-reinforcing 'compliance economy' that draws talent away from productive work; rent-seeking has increasing returns, so Europe needs a regulatory pause, sunset clauses and one-in-one-out rules.
original_source: authors' own analysis (drawing on Murphy, Shleifer and Vishny 1991/1993; Baumol 1990)

text: The CSRD covers about 42,000 companies, which must report on 1,052 data points, 783 of them mandatory.
CSRD compliance costs range from EUR 150,000 for non-listed companies to EUR 1m for listed ones.
A Danish government analysis puts the minimum CSRD compliance cost at EUR 300,000 a year per company and EUR 365,000 in the first year.
original_source: Danish government estimate, cited in Draghi report, Part B (2024), https://commission.europa.eu/topics/strengthening-european-competitiveness/eu-competitiveness-looking-ahead_en (p.318)
verified: original source differs: Draghi Part B (fn 22) gives average one-off costs of EUR 365,000 and recurring costs of EUR 310,000 a year (survey of 2,200 firms, a floor), not EUR 300,000

text: CEA-PME estimates the initial CSRD cost for a French mid-cap at over EUR 800,000 over two years.
original_source: CEA-PME, cited in Draghi report, Part B (2024), https://commission.europa.eu/topics/strengthening-european-competitiveness/eu-competitiveness-looking-ahead_en

text: CSRD compliance costs for mid-caps reach 12.5% of their investment volume.
original_source: EIB and EPC study 'Hidden Champions, Missed Opportunities', cited in Draghi report, Part B (2024), https://commission.europa.eu/topics/strengthening-european-competitiveness/eu-competitiveness-looking-ahead_en (p.321)

text: In Denmark the number of rules (Danish and EU) applying to the average firm rose by 63% between 2001 and 2023.
Annual compliance costs for a chemical-industry SME almost doubled from EUR 332,500 in 2014 to EUR 577,000 in 2023.
GDPR compliance costs run from EUR 500,000 for SMEs to EUR 10m for large organisations.

EU law adds to national law instead of replacing it; the post says the duplication costs about EUR 200bn a year (complex procedures, excess national requirements, unharmonised labelling). In Draghi this is the opportunity cost of a lack of harmonisation.
KPMG: only 29% of companies feel they have the ESG policies, skills and systems needed for independent ESG data assurance.
Spain set up Europe's first national AI supervisory agency (AESIA), with a president, director, two subdirectors, a secretary general and 10 departments, even though Spain has no frontier AI firms.

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: The AI Act heaps heavy duties on 'high-risk' uses and large general-purpose models, and leaves enforcement to dozens of national authorities. This fragments the market, favours incumbents and penalises the agentic AI where the gains are largest, so it should be rewritten now rather than at the 2029 review.

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Before release, a high-risk AI system (e.g. an AI tutor) must meet about 16 separate obligations: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, cybersecurity, quality management, 10-year record-keeping, an EU representative, conformity assessment, fundamental-rights impact assessment, declaration of conformity and EU database registration.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 (Arts 9-49)

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Fines reach the higher of EUR 35m or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices, and EUR 15m or 3% for other breaches.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 (Art. 99)
verified: original source checked (Art. 99(3) EUR 35,000,000 or 7%; Art. 99(4) EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher)

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Decisions based on remote biometric identification must be separately verified by at least two natural persons; the post illustrates this with an 'AI bank teller'.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 (recital, p.21; Art. 14(5))

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: A general-purpose model is presumed to pose 'systemic risk' above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute, a threshold already passed by GPT-4, Gemini and Llama 3.1, or if the Commission designates it.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 (Art. 51)

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Enforcement will involve at least 50 to 55+ bodies: four EU-level bodies (AI Office, Board, scientific panel, advisory forum) plus at least one market surveillance authority, one notifying authority and notified bodies in each of the 27 member states.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 (Arts 64-70)

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: About 60-70 further pieces of secondary legislation will be needed to fully implement the AI Act.

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Phase-in: prohibitions from February 2025, general-purpose AI rules from August 2025, high-risk requirements from August 2026; a Commission review is set for 2029.
original_source: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (article cited in post), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689

post_title: The Strange Kafka World of the EU AI Act
text: Compliance is a large fixed cost that pushes concentration ('a $1 million machine to make cookies'), so incumbents like Meta or Microsoft can handle 27+ market surveillance authorities while start-ups cannot. Meta cites data protection and Apple cites the DMA for holding back products in Europe.

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: GDPR spread privacy norms (the intended Brussels effect), but the evidence shows it raised data costs, concentrated markets in favour of Google and Facebook, and cut app entry and VC investment, which is especially harmful for AI. It should be revised, aligned with the CCPA, enforced from Brussels alone and evaluated regularly.

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Survey estimates of GDPR compliance costs range from $1.3m for small companies to $70m for larger ones.

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Structural estimates suggest GDPR made data storage 20% more costly for EU firms; two years on, EU firms stored 26% less data than US firms and cut computation by 15% relative to US firms.
original_source: Demirer, Jimenez Hernandez, Li and Peng (2024), NBER w32146

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Web traffic and online tracking fell by 10-15% after GDPR took effect.
original_source: Goldberg, Johnson and Shriver (2024), AEJ: Economic Policy

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Member states can set their own privacy rules in 15 areas under GDPR, fragmenting enforcement.

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: The EU has around 100 tech-focused laws and more than 270 regulators active in digital networks across member states.
verified: original source checked (Draghi Part A: 'around 100 tech-focused laws and over 270 regulators active in digital networks across all Member States')

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: GDPR led to the exit of about a third of available apps on Google Play, and new app entry fell by half in the following quarters; average users per app rose by about a quarter for post-GDPR apps.
original_source: Janssen, Kesler, Kummer and Waldfogel (2022), NBER w30028, https://www.nber.org/papers/w30028
verified: original source checked (NBER abstract: 'exit of about a third of available apps ... entry of new apps fell by half'; data on 4.1m apps 2016-2019)

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Monthly venture deals in the EU fell by 26.1% relative to the US and 34.2% relative to the rest of the world after GDPR; data-intensive ventures fell about 31%; deals for early-stage firms fell 34% and for young (0-3 year) firms 30.3% relative to the US.
original_source: Jia, Jin and Wagman (2021), Marketing Science, https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2020.1271
verified: original source differs: the open NBER working-paper version (w25248, Nov 2018) reports a 17.6% fall in weekly EU venture deals and a 39.6% fall in amount per deal vs the US. The 26.1%/34.2% monthly figures presumably come from the published 2021 version (paywalled, not checked).

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Market concentration among web technology vendors rose by 17% after GDPR, with Google and Facebook gaining share; Peukert et al. find Google lost relatively less and gained share in advertising.
original_source: Johnson, Shriver and Goldberg (2023), Management Science; Peukert et al. (2022), Marketing Science

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: Anecdote: a small Spanish B2B firm's contact database fell from 300,000 firms to 15,000 the day GDPR began, because explicit consent was required.

post_title: Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe?
text: GDPR fines can reach 4% of global revenue.

Europe has indulged in 'luxury rules', virtuous but growth-reducing policies on energy, tech regulation (GDPR, AI Act) and cars, that it could afford only while relying on the US for security and innovation. Strategic autonomy now requires giving them up.
Europe has not built from scratch a single company worth over EUR 100bn in the last 50 years, while the US created six worth over EUR 1 trillion in the same period.
The EU passed around 13,000 acts in 2019-2024, against about 3,500 laws and 2,000 resolutions at US federal level.
The EU targets a 55% emissions cut from 1990 levels by 2030; the US has a soft 50-52% target from a higher 2005 baseline, and China aims only for a peak in 2030.
The EU builds 12 different types of battle tanks while the US makes one.

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: The leaked 28th-regime (EU Inc.) proposal is incorporated nationally, subject to national law and notarial control, so it would amount to '27 different 28th regimes', as happened with the SE. A narrower regime for young, cross-border scalable firms could carry real substance (one registry, standard documents, one VAT channel, EU stock options).

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: The leaked proposal allows digital incorporation within 48 hours for at most EUR 100; its impact assessment reportedly estimates burden savings of about EUR 400m over ten years, which the authors call 'a rounding error'.

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: The European Parliament backed a 28th regime by 492 votes to 144.

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: Of 147 European unicorns founded between 2008 and 2021, 40 relocated their headquarters abroad, mostly to the US.
verified: original source checked (Draghi Part A p.29: '147 unicorns were founded in Europe ... 40 of these have relocated their headquarters abroad, with the vast majority moving' to the US)

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: Of 23 million EU corporations, only a few thousand are European Companies (SEs), because the 2004 statute defers so much to national law.

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: When the US let companies bypass state securities laws through federal regulation, late-stage firms became four times more likely to attract out-of-state investors.

post_title: Calling something the 28th regime does not make it one
text: The 28th regime is meant to give firms access to 450 million consumers through a single set of rules.

The auto omnibus softens the 2035 combustion ban only by tying the remaining emissions to 'Made in Europe' green steel and renewable fuel credits, adds new country-specific quotas for corporate fleets and protectionist sourcing rules, and shows that the Commission that wrote the green rules keeps writing more.
The proposal lowers the required 2035 fleet emissions cut from 100% to 90% of 2021 levels; carmakers have cut emissions by only 7% so far.

60% of cars and 90% of vans in Europe are company-owned or leased; new binding targets require e.g. 90% low/zero-emission leased vehicles in the Netherlands by 2030 (48% in Greece) and 95% zero-emission in the Netherlands and Germany by 2035 (56% in Portugal and Poland).
France wants automakers obliged to source at least 75% of electric-car parts in Europe.

The Competitiveness Compass makes the case for growth but denies trade-offs, comes without money, adds plans and regulation (such as a Circular Economy Act) instead of removing burdens, and ignores the AI Act. The 28th regime is its best idea, but thresholds risk keeping firms small.
By the authors' count, 36 pieces of environmental legislation were passed in 2019-24 (elsewhere in the post 38); a Circular Economy Act would be the 37th.
Size thresholds distort firm growth: when a rule starts at 50 workers, firms bunch below 50.
original_source: Garicano, Lelarge and Van Reenen (2016), American Economic Review

text: Nuclear and storage are mentioned zero times in the Compass; eight sectoral 'action plans' are referenced.

Politicians 'entangle' the economic and environmental sides of climate policy: supporters deny its costs and opponents deny its benefits. When costs rise, opponents question the benefits, so policy support swings sharply and collapses once 'the bill arrives'.
original_source: Brzezinski and Garicano (2025), 'Narrative Entanglement in Climate Policy', CEPR DP 20829, https://drive.google.com/file/d/1K_Awui9EPmQxiqqa5uXFnZw6FiIRZAbM/view

text: In an LLM analysis of tens of thousands of speeches in the 9th European Parliament (2019-2024), over 80% of climate speeches were 'entangled'; after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, speeches were 80% more likely to say climate policy is not needed.

EU plans such as the Union of Skills fail because the Commission, a consensus coalition, writes policy as if there were no losers and cannot take on the interest groups that block reform; Europe's priorities still favour entrenched groups over innovation.
By 2022 about one third of EU 15-year-olds lacked minimum proficiency in mathematics and a quarter struggled with reading.
original_source: European Commission, Union of Skills communication, https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/document/download/915b147d-c5af-44bb-9820-c252d872fd31_en

text: The Commission plans to invest EUR 4bn in AI by 2027, while the EU spends EUR 55bn a year on farm subsidies.

Defense shows the cost of Europe's 'luxury rules': ESG financing exclusions, planning, civil aviation and procurement rules stop defense firms from building quickly or cheaply, so extra budgets buy little capacity.
40% of European defense companies find access to finance very difficult, compared with 6.6% of companies overall.
original_source: European Commission study on access to equity financing for defence SMEs (2024), https://defence-industry-space.ec.europa.eu/study-results-access-equity-financing-european-defence-smes-2024-01-11_en

text: Until April 2024 the EIB required dual-use projects to earn over 50% of revenue from civilian uses; weapons remain excluded.

The Patroller drone took 14 years from design to first delivery, partly because of civilian rules on flights over populated areas; the Bundestag budget committee must approve any defense contract above EUR 25m.
original_source: French National Assembly defence committee hearing, https://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/dyn/17/comptes-rendus/cion_def/l17cion_def2425024_compte-rendu

text: European defense budgets reach about EUR 336bn; a 20mm shell casing takes 6-8 weeks to produce in France versus under 2 weeks in Ukraine.
original_source: authors' own analysis (sources partly linked: RFE/RL, Bloomberg)

text: The DSA targets content violations (fines up to 6% of global revenue) but offers no tool against platforms controlled by a 'systemic rival': restricting TikTok would require a criminal threat to life or safety. Europe should target media ownership by countries of concern.

Since 2022 platforms in Europe are liable for numerous forms of harmful content under the DSA, with fines up to 6% of global revenue (Art. 52(3)); temporary access restrictions (Art. 51(3)) need a criminal offence threatening life or safety.
TikTok reaches about 150 million Europeans and commands about 50 billion hours of European attention a year; one DSA investigation centres on 25,000 Russian bots in the Romanian election.
original_source: authors' own analysis; BBC on bots, https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm2v13nz202o
